newsitem.title: USA: White House promises aid for "dilapidated" D.C.
newsitem.headline: White House promises aid for "dilapidated" D.C.

text.p: White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta on Sunday declared the nation's capital "weak and dilapidated" and said President Bill Clinton was committed to tackling the city's dire financial problems.

"We all have a responsibility to ensure we do what we can to make the city a centerpiece for the country rather than the kind of weak, dilapidated problem we are seeing," he said on the NBC program "Meet the Press."

Panettta, who plans to return soon to his California home, said the District of Columbia posed "a tough challenge" but that the federal government did not want to make "pie-in-the-sky promises" it could not keep.

"The city's been through too much ... we understand the responsibility we have, the real question is what do we do and can it be done within budget restraints," Panetta said. "It's a concern to everyone and particularly the president."

Panetta said several agencies were working on where the federal government could ease the district's burden and he predicted any rescue package would include financial assistance and tax incentives. But he appeared to reject the idea of a big tax cut or a flat tax rate for the district, saying it posed "real concern."
Panetta said there was "no question" that Clinton would authorize some help to the capital. "He is committed," the chief of staff said.
The district's budgetary chaos stems from its confusing role as part city, part state in which it has to provide the services of both without financial recourse to a state government.
Clinton on Friday described its budgetary chaos as "a series of purgatories" complicated by the city's unique status as "not quite independent and not quite dependent."
"And very often, when responsibilities are divided, they end up being nobody's responsibility," he said.

A five-member board appointed by Congress in 1995 to oversee the District's finances has recommended the federal government take over about $1 billion worth of the city's programs that are typically paid for by states.

The board's plan warned that the district would not emerge from mounting financial crisis unless the U.S. government took over funding such programs as Medicaid, mental health care, prisons and road maintenance. Cities usually pass those costs on to their states.
Behind its tourist attractions -- the White House, the monuments and the museums -- Washington is a troubled city with a rapidly declining population of 570,000, many poor and black.

For most of its history, the 10-mile-square (16 km-square) enclave that came to be called the District of Columbia was controlled by the federal government and Congress. However, in 1974 Congress relinquished that power, awarded the district financial independence -- or home rule -- and the right to vote for a mayor and city council.

The city is in serious financial trouble with a bloated bureaucracy, crumbling services and a collapsing school system. It faces a budget shortfall of $85 million this year that must be met through aggressive cuts in spending and personnel.

But the district already is short of fire trucks and emergency vehicles; police cars go unrepaired, potholes unfilled; crime flourishes and a U.S. army general was recently appointed by the board to run its schools.
